speciesDescription:
Small birds of mud, reeds, and shallow edges.

This group includes my shorebirds — Killdeer, Dunlins, yellowlegs, sandpipers and plovers — plus my secretive marsh birds — rails, Common Gallinule, and American Coot.

I love photographing them because you have to get low, be patient, and watch closely. A Killdeer faking a broken wing on gravel, a Dunlin probing the mudflat, a gallinule stepping across lily pads — tough little birds making a living where marsh and city meet.
title: Birds (d): Marsh and Shorebirds

speciesDescription:
The vibrant members of the blackbird family bring a splash of color to the Meadowlands. From the sunny bursts of the Baltimore Oriole to the iridescent hues of the Common Grackle, this gallery showcases these remarkable birds.

You'll find them in trees and marshes, foraging for insects and berries, and often singing with exuberance. Explore these images to witness their stunning plumage and dynamic behaviors that make them a joy to observe and photograph.

seo.metaTitle: Wrens | The Meadow Lens

speciesDescription:
Small, brown, and louder than they have any right to be — wrens are big personalities in small packages!

The Carolina Wren and House Wren live along brush piles, thickets, and marsh edges. The Carolina belts out its tea-kettle, tea-kettle song year-round, while the summer-visiting House Wren answers with a bubbly, chattering cascade.

The Marsh Wren is a bit different. It lives deeper in the reeds and cattails, clinging to vertical stems and singing a buzzy, rattling song you hear more often than you see the bird. I love (that's a stretch btw!) photographing it because you have to be (insanely) patient and quiet to catch it popping up for just a second. Then you have to press the shutter in time! The end result is worth it though... they're adorable!
title: Wrens

quote: Laughter and Nature is the best medicine!

children.text: I am David McClure, a fine art photographer with a lifelong passion for capturing the raw, uninterrupted beauty of nature. For years, I have explored the hidden depths of the New Jersey Meadowlands and beyond, waiting for those fleeting moments of perfection.

This gallery is a curated exhibition of my life's work — from the aggressive grace of birds of prey to the tranquil stillness of untouched vistas. I invite you to step into these digital halls and explore the world through my lens.

children.text: Welcome to the complete digital overhaul of The Meadow Lens. I have rebuilt the entire gallery from the ground up to provide a more immersive, high-resolution viewing experience for my collectors. The new platform features expansive "Exhibition Rooms", advanced sorting by species and color, and a seamless interface for private inquiries.

title: The New Meadow Lens Gallery is Live

children.text: This past weekend I spent 14 hours stationed near Exit 16W, documenting the early migratory patterns of the local raptor population. The atmospheric haze from the city provided an incredible backdrop for the shots. I am currently editing this series and will be adding the first few limited editions to the "Birds" collection next week.

While I am known primarily for avian photography, I have been turning my macro lens toward the fascinating insect life thriving in the protected lands. The "Flora and Fauna" categories have just been updated with several new high-contrast studies.

This gallery is about birds and animals living in the "built environment" — hawks hunting over parking lots, killdeer nesting on gravel, swallows under bridges, sparrows bathing in street puddles, herons with the skyline behind them and jets overhead.

seo.metaTitle: Cedar Waxwing | The Meadow Lens

speciesDescription: Sleek, silky, and almost too perfect... Cedar Waxwings. If Cardinals are a flash of color, Cedar Waxwings are pure elegance. They move through berry bushes and trees, passing berries to each other and calling with that soft, high hissing sound. Seeing just one is a treat, but seeing several is pure joy! They don't stay for very many weeks, so having these photos as evidence of their beauty is a true privilege!
title: Cedar Waxwing

seo.metaTitle: Belted Kingfisher | The Meadow Lens

speciesDescription:
Loud, fast, and impossible to miss once you know the call — the Belted Kingfisher is a Meadowlands favorite.

Perched on wires, posts, and reeds along our tidal creeks, it announces itself with a harsh, rattling cry, then hovers and plunge-dives headfirst for fish. I love photographing it because you hear it long before you see it, and the dive happens in a split second. Look for the shaggy crest, big bill, and blue-gray band — females have an extra rusty-red belt.
title: Belted Kingfisher

seo.metaTitle: Northern Cardinal | The Meadow Lens

speciesDescription: The Northern Cardinal is one of the most rewarding birds to behold — and photograph. A flash of red against green reeds, brown cattails, winter snow, or a blue-gray dusk skyline is unforgettable. Cardinals provide natural color contrast that photographs beautifully. A Cardinal singing with reeds in front and the city behind captures exactly what The Meadow Lens is about: wild beauty persisting in an urban landscape. Then there's the spiritual belief that seeing a Cardinal makes one feel that a lost love one is near or watching over them. I hope these images of Cardinals provide at least one of these good benefits for you!
title: Northern Cardinal

seo.metaTitle: Birds (a): Songbirds | The Meadow Lens

speciesDescription:
Small birds, big personalities — the singers and neighbors of the marsh edge.

This group includes my wrens including Carolina, House, and Marsh Wrens, thrushes like Robin, Hermit Thrush and Wood Thrush, sparrows, finches, warblers including Northern and Louisiana Waterthrush, vireos, chickadees, kinglets, titmice, corvids, blackbirds and starlings, buntings, Northern Cardinal, mimicking birds, woodpeckers, and swallows.

I love photographing them because you earn the shot — waiting by a brush pile or cattail edge for that cocked tail, tilted head, or burst of song.
title: Birds (a): Songbirds

seo.metaTitle: Birds (b): Raptors | The Meadow Lens

speciesDescription:
Power, patience, and precision — the hunters of the Meadowlands sky.

This group includes my eagles, hawks, harriers, osprey, falcons including the American Kestrel, and owls. Bald Eagles over the marsh, Red-tailed Hawks on light poles, Northern Harriers gliding low over reeds, Peregrine Falcons on bridges, kestrels hovering over fields.

I photograph them for that moment when waiting turns to action — wildness thriving with jets, highways, and skyline in the same frame.
title: Birds (b): Raptors

seo.metaDescription: Explore the Birds fine art photography exhibition across 20 specialized sub-venues, captured in the New Jersey Meadowlands by David McClure.
seo.metaTitle: Birds (c): Waterbirds | The Meadow Lens

speciesDescription:
This is life on open water in the Meadowlands — our tidal creeks, ponds, reservoirs, and the Hudson.

This group includes my waders like herons and egrets, waterfowl like ducks, geese and swans, diving waterbirds like loons, grebes and cormorants, plus gulls, terns, skimmers, and the Belted Kingfisher.

I love photographing them here because the wild and the urban share the same frame — a Great Egret striking at fish, a Bufflehead diving in winter light, a cormorant drying its wings on a piling with the skyline behind it.
title: Birds (c): Waterbirds

speciesDescription:
Secretive, slender, and easy to hear but hard to see — cuckoos are a special find in the Meadowlands.

These photos are Yellow-billed Cuckoos, found in our deciduous woods and thickets hunting large caterpillars. Look for the long tail with bold white spots underneath, curved yellow bill, and warm rufous wings in flight.
title: Birds (f): Cuckoos
